posts.title: Benchmark coding agents on your own repo
posts.promise: Compare agent results on a few repeatable tasks from merged changes.
posts.whatItIs: SelfBench turns a repository’s merged pull requests into benchmark tasks, runs coding agents against them, then compares accuracy and cost. Its README says an authoring agent creates hidden tests and a reference solution, and accepted tasks must pass checks and independent review. A beginner could build a much smaller version for one open repository: choose a few merged changes, create a task and basic tests, run one or two agents in a disposable sandbox, and record results.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: engineering teams evaluating coding agents may pay for repository-specific comparisons; the supplied sources do not establish paying customers or revenue.
loop: Connect one test repository and select a few merged pull requests.
Draft a task statement from each change.
Generate hidden tests and a reference solution for human review.
Run selected agents against approved tasks in isolated sandboxes.
Record pass rate and run cost in a small comparison table.
A maintainer checks flawed tasks and interprets ambiguous results.
posts.evidence: The public README describes a web app, repository-specific tasks from merged pull requests, generated hidden tests, agent runs, and live leaderboards for named open-source repositories. It says tasks are reviewed and approved; this is first-party product documentation, not independent validation of customers or revenue.
posts.uncertainty: This is a real documented product example, but the proposed student version is hypothetical. Test generation can be wrong, and agent runs need safe isolation, human task approval, and interpretation. The sources do not prove demand, paid use, benchmark validity across repositories, or unattended operation.
first24Hours: Choose a small public repository with several understandable merged changes.
Manually turn one change into a task and write a simple pass/fail test.
Run two available coding agents in disposable copies and note where human review changes the result.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: engineering teams may pay for repository-specific model comparisons; demand and revenue are unproved.

feasibility.reason: A small prototype can benchmark a few merged changes, but safe sandboxes and hidden-test quality constrain scope.

autonomy.reason: Task generation and agent runs can repeat; README says people approve each generated evaluation and review results.

evidence.reason: README documents an app workflow and public live leaderboards for repositories; it does not establish paying use.

steps.message: Assessed all 12 selected leads against first-party or supplied evidence and prior decisions. SelfBench is the only lead provisionally at the threshold: the README documents a repeatable repo-benchmark workflow and its human approval gate; demand remains hypothetical.
